A UK coroner has ruled that punitive school rules and a relationship breakdown contributed to the death of a 15-year-old pupil who struggled with his school’s disciplinary policies. The pupil, identified as Taylor Lee, from Plymouth, died in November 2023 after repeatedly complaining that attending school had become an exhausting daily struggle. An inquest at Devon Coroner’s Court in Exeter heard that Taylor had criticised the strict behaviour policies introduced by Ivybridge Community College, where he was a Year 11 student. According to a report by the Daily Mail on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, the school had introduced an isolation policy under which pupils faced punishment for arriving late to lessons. On one occasion, Taylor was reportedly sent for reflection after arriving 47 seconds late to class. He also criticised the school’s disciplinary measures, describing its behaviour policies as “unlogical” and expressing concern about their emotional impact on other pupils. Taylor was subsequently suspended after challenging the rules during a confrontation with his headteacher. Following his return, he again raised concerns, prompting the school to allow pupils an additional minute to get to their lessons. Make PUNCH part of your everyday experience. Area Coroner Alison Longhorn recorded a conclusion of suicide, identifying the school’s disciplinary approach and the breakdown of Taylor’s relationship with his girlfriend as contributing factors. She said Taylor’s experience at school had “a most significant impact” which more than minimally contributed to his death. The coroner also disclosed that the teenager had previously experienced mental health difficulties, including low mood and self-harm. He had struggled with bullying, mock GCSE examinations and his relationships with some teachers. During the inquest, the school’s principal, Rachel Hutchinson, described Taylor as a “charismatic, very creative” pupil who loved life and music. However, she said he was “a complex character” who struggled with school routines and expectations. She explained that the stricter disciplinary measures were introduced following increased school absences after the COVID-19 pandemic. The measures included a bell system to prompt pupils to attend lessons, a six-minute window to move between classes and sanctions for lateness, mobile phone use and other breaches of school rules. Hutchinson said the policies remained in place. The coroner expressed concern that the same situation could arise again, noting that there had been no changes to the college’s policies since Taylor’s death. She also highlighted a missed opportunity after a police officer who had dealt with Taylor warned the school about his fragile mental state but received no response. The coroner said she would issue a Prevention of Future Deaths report to address the concerns raised during the inquest. Youth worker Richard Brooks told the inquest that Taylor had been disengaged from education and unhappy with the school’s rules. He recalled the teenager telling him: “Every day is a battle and exhausting.” The principal also said investigations by Ofsted and Devon County Council following complaints about the school’s policies had concluded that no further action was necessary.
